title: Cramer's Rule & More Determinant Properties
description: Practice det(AB) = det(A)det(B), det(A⁻¹) = 1/det(A), the invertibility test, the adjoint formula for A⁻¹, and conceptual Cramer's Rule (Anton §2.3).

questions.prompt: det(A) = 4 and det(B) = 5. What is det(AB)?
det(A) = -3 and det(B) = 7. What is det(AB)?
det(A) = 6 and det(B) = -2. What is det(AB)?
det(A) = -4 and det(B) = -5. What is det(AB)?
questions.explanation: det(AB) = det(A)·det(B) = -4 × -5 = 20 (two negatives make a positive).

questions.prompt: det(AB) = 30 and det(A) = 6. What is det(B)?
det(AB) = -24 and det(B) = 8. What is det(A)?
det(A) = 2, det(B) = 2, det(C) = 3, all the same size. What is det(ABC)?
questions.explanation: Apply det(AB) = det(A)det(B) twice: det(ABC) = det(A)·det(B)·det(C) = 2 × 2 × 3 = 12.

questions.prompt: A is a 3×3 matrix with det(A) = 5. What is det(A²)?
det(A) = 4. What is det(A⁻¹)?
det(A) = -2. What is det(A⁻¹)?
det(A) = 10. What is det(A⁻¹)?
det(A⁻¹) = 1/7. What is det(A)?
questions.explanation: Since det(A⁻¹) = 1/det(A), det(A) is the reciprocal of 1/7, which is 7.

questions.prompt: det(A⁻¹) = -1/3. What is det(A)?
questions.explanation: Since det(A⁻¹) = 1/det(A), det(A) is the reciprocal of -1/3, which is -3.

questions.prompt: det(A) = 1. What is det(A⁻¹)?
True or False: if det(A) = 0, then A is invertible.
explanations: A zero determinant is exactly the invertibility test failing — A is NOT invertible.

questions.prompt: det(A) = 0 for a square matrix A. What can you conclude?
choices: None of the above are guaranteed
explanations: It's the opposite — a zero determinant rules out invertibility.
If A isn't invertible, A⁻¹ doesn't exist, so det(A⁻¹) can't either.
The invertibility test gives a definite answer here: not invertible.

questions.prompt: True or False: a matrix with two proportional (parallel) rows must have determinant 0.
explanations: Two proportional rows make the matrix singular — its determinant is always 0.

questions.prompt: Which of the following guarantees A is NOT invertible?
explanations: A nonzero determinant means A IS invertible.
A nonzero determinant (even negative) means A IS invertible.
A nonzero determinant means A IS invertible.

questions.prompt: True or False: if A is invertible, then A⁻¹ is also invertible.
explanations: det(A⁻¹) = 1/det(A), which is nonzero whenever det(A) is — so A⁻¹ passes the invertibility test too.

questions.prompt: A is a 4×4 matrix with det(A) = 0. Which is true?
choices: A must be the zero matrix
explanations: There's no such thing as an inverse equal to the zero matrix — A⁻¹ simply doesn't exist here.
If A⁻¹ doesn't exist, det(A⁻¹) isn't defined at all — it's not 0.
Plenty of nonzero matrices have determinant 0 — a repeated or dependent row is enough.

questions.prompt: The adjoint (adjugate) of A is the _____ of the matrix of cofactors.
questions.explanation: adj(A)ᵢⱼ = Cⱼᵢ — the cofactor matrix gets transposed to form the adjoint.

questions.prompt: The formula A⁻¹ = (1/det A)·adj(A) is valid exactly when...
explanations: Being square is necessary just to have a determinant at all, but it's not the condition that makes the formula work.
The formula works for any invertible matrix, symmetric or not.
The formula works for any invertible matrix, triangular or not.

questions.prompt: For A = [a,b; c,d], adj(A) equals
explanations: The off-diagonal entries need their signs flipped, not just left alone.
It's the diagonal entries that swap places, not the off-diagonal signs.
Close in spirit, but the diagonal entries swap positions rather than just the sign pattern shown here.

questions.prompt: A = [5,2; 3,1]. What is det(A)?
A = [5,2; 3,1]. Using the adjoint formula, what is the (1,1) entry of A⁻¹?
A = [5,2; 3,1]. Using the adjoint formula, what is the (2,2) entry of A⁻¹?
True or False: the adjoint formula for A⁻¹ is usually the fastest method for large matrices.
explanations: Computing every cofactor gets expensive fast — row reduction is the practical method for anything bigger than 2×2 or 3×3.

questions.prompt: The cofactor Cᵢⱼ of entry aᵢⱼ is (−1)ⁱ⁺ʲ times the determinant of the _____ formed by deleting row i and column j.
questions.explanation: Deleting row i and column j leaves a smaller submatrix (minor); the cofactor is its determinant, with a sign attached.

questions.prompt: Cramer's Rule requires which condition on A to apply?
explanations: Cramer's Rule doesn't care about symmetry.
Cramer's Rule works for any square A with a nonzero determinant, not just triangular ones.
The sign or size of A's entries doesn't matter — only whether det(A) ≠ 0.

questions.prompt: In Cramer's Rule, Aᵢ is the matrix A with column i replaced by _____.
questions.explanation: Aᵢ swaps out column i of A for the right-hand-side vector b; then xᵢ = det(Aᵢ)/det(A).

questions.prompt: True or False: Cramer's Rule can be used even when det(A) = 0 — you just get xᵢ = 0/0.
explanations: Division by det(A) = 0 is undefined — Cramer's Rule simply doesn't apply, it doesn't produce 0/0 as a usable answer.

questions.prompt: For Ax = b with det(A) = 6, det(A₁) = 18, det(A₂) = -12. What is x₁?
explanations: That's det(A)/det(A₁), upside down — Cramer's Rule is xᵢ = det(Aᵢ)/det(A).
That's det(A₁) + det(A), not the ratio Cramer's Rule asks for.
That's det(A₁)×det(A), not the ratio Cramer's Rule asks for.

questions.prompt: For Ax = b with det(A) = 6, det(A₁) = 18, det(A₂) = -12. What is x₂?
Cramer's Rule is most practical for...
choices: small systems, especially by hand (2×2 or 3×3)
systems where A is not square
explanations: Computing that many determinants by cofactor expansion is far too slow — row reduction wins for large systems.
Cramer's Rule assumes a unique solution exists (det(A) ≠ 0) — it isn't a tool for systems with no solution.
Cramer's Rule requires a square coefficient matrix A.

questions.prompt: True or False: Cramer's Rule and row reduction always give the same solution when both apply.
explanations: They're two different methods for the same system — when a unique solution exists, both must find it.

questions.prompt: For a 2×2 system with det(A) = 5 and det(Aₓ) = -15, what is x?
If det(A) = 0 for the coefficient matrix of Ax = b, the system has...
choices: exactly one solution, found by Cramer's Rule
no solution or infinitely many solutions
always infinitely many solutions, never zero
explanations: det(A) = 0 is exactly the case where Cramer's Rule does NOT apply — there's no unique solution to find this way.
Whether a solution exists at all depends on b, but it isn't as simple as requiring b = 0.
It could be no solution OR infinitely many, depending on b — not always the latter.

questions.prompt: True or False: Cramer's Rule directly generalizes to any size square system, not just 2×2 and 3×3.
explanations: The formula xᵢ = det(Aᵢ)/det(A) works for any n×n system with det(A) ≠ 0 — it's just increasingly impractical to compute by hand as n grows.

questions.prompt: True or False: det(AB) = det(BA) for square matrices A, B of the same size, even though AB ≠ BA in general.
explanations: det(AB) = det(A)det(B) = det(B)det(A) = det(BA) — ordinary number multiplication commutes even when matrix multiplication doesn't.

questions.prompt: True or False: det(A + B) = det(A) + det(B) in general.
explanations: Determinants don't distribute over addition. Example: A = B = I (2×2): det(A)+det(B) = 1+1 = 2, but det(A+B) = det(2I) = 4.

questions.prompt: det(kA) = kⁿ·det(A) for an n×n matrix A — the exponent n appears because scaling A by k scales _____ row(s).
questions.explanation: Multiplying A by the scalar k multiplies every one of its n rows by k, contributing one factor of k each — so the total factor is kⁿ.

questions.prompt: True or False: det(Aᵀ) = det(A) for every square matrix A.
explanations: Transposing swaps rows and columns, but every determinant property that holds for rows also holds for columns — the determinant is unchanged.

questions.prompt: A is 3×3 with det(A) = 2. What is det(A³)?
explanations: Determinants of repeated products multiply, they don't add.
det(A³) ≠ det(A) — cubing the matrix does change the determinant.
That would be det(A⁻³), not det(A³).

questions.prompt: A is 5×5 with det(A) = -1. What is det(-A)?
True or False: if A and B are both invertible n×n matrices, then AB is also invertible.
explanations: det(AB) = det(A)det(B), and a product of two nonzero numbers is nonzero — so det(AB) ≠ 0.

questions.prompt: det(A) = 3 and det(B) = 0. What is det(AB)?
explanations: det(AB) = det(A)det(B), and multiplying by 0 doesn't leave det(A) unchanged.
det(AB) is perfectly well-defined — it's just 0.
There's no sign flip here, just multiplication by 0.

questions.prompt: Since det(A)·det(A⁻¹) = 1, if det(A) is very close to 0, det(A⁻¹) will be very _____.
questions.explanation: det(A⁻¹) = 1/det(A) — dividing 1 by a number close to 0 produces a very large result.

questions.prompt: True or False: every invertible matrix has a unique inverse.
explanations: If A had two different inverses B and C, then B = BI = B(AC) = (BA)C = IC = C — contradiction. The inverse is always unique.

questions.prompt: A is 4×4 with det(A) = 2. What is det(2A)?
Which single fact explains ALL of: the invertibility test, the adjoint formula, and det(A⁻¹) = 1/det(A)?
explanations: Being square is required just to define det(A) — it's not what ties these three facts together.
None of the three facts depend on the sign of A's entries.
None of the three facts require A to be triangular.

questions.prompt: det(A) = 7 and det(B) = 1/7. What is det(AB)?
A is invertible. Which of the following is FALSE?
explanations: This is true — it's the definition of invertible via the determinant test.
This is true — that's what invertible means.
This is true — it's the reciprocal relationship proved in class.

questions.prompt: True or False: adj(A) is defined even when A is not invertible (det(A) = 0).
explanations: The adjugate is just the transposed cofactor matrix — it always exists. It's the FORMULA A⁻¹ = adj(A)/det(A) that breaks down when det(A) = 0, not adj(A) itself.

questions.prompt: For an n×n matrix, adj(A) is built from the _____ matrix, then transposed.
questions.explanation: adj(A) is the transpose of the cofactor matrix: adj(A)ᵢⱼ = Cⱼᵢ.

questions.prompt: A = [2,0; 0,3]. Using the adjoint formula, what is the (2,2) entry of A⁻¹?
questions.explanation: det(A) = 6, adj(A) = [3,0; 0,2], so A⁻¹ = (1/6)[3,0; 0,2] = [1/2,0; 0,1/3]. The (2,2) entry is 1/3 — matching the direct inverse of a diagonal matrix.

questions.prompt: Cramer's Rule computes xᵢ as a ratio of two...
explanations: Cramer's Rule doesn't involve the trace at all.
Rank doesn't enter the Cramer's Rule formula.
Eigenvalues aren't part of the Cramer's Rule formula.

questions.prompt: True or False: in Cramer's Rule, det(A) (the denominator) is the same for every xᵢ in the system.
explanations: Only the numerator det(Aᵢ) changes from one variable to the next — the denominator det(A) is fixed for the whole system.

questions.prompt: A is 2×2 with det(A) = -6. What is det(A⁻¹)?
You're told det(A) = 0 for a system's coefficient matrix. Besides Cramer's Rule failing, what else do you know from the invertibility test?
choices: The system has exactly one solution
explanations: The opposite is true — det(A) = 0 means A is NOT invertible.
adj(A) still exists (it's just cofactors and a transpose) — it's A⁻¹ = adj(A)/det(A) that fails.
det(A) = 0 rules out a unique solution — the system has either no solution or infinitely many.

questions.prompt: True or False: det(AB) = det(A)·det(B) requires A and B to both be square matrices of the same size.
explanations: The rule is stated for square matrices of matching size — that's exactly when both AB and BA are defined and square, and determinants make sense for all of them.
